prompt: Put the reviewer's path through a GitHub profile in order.
How many repositories does the lesson say to pin?

choices.text: All six slots, filled with whatever is most recent
None, since pinning hides the other repositories
choices.why: Pinning is how the evidence shows first.

choices.text: One to three, the ones that are evidence
Only forks

prompt: What must the few lines above the repositories say, by the lesson?

choices.text: A list of every language you have ever written a line in, with a badge for each
Your date of birth
A quote that sums up how you approach technical work
Who you are and what you do

prompt: What does a pinned repository need, by the lesson?
hint: The cheapest line to get right.

choices.text: At least a hundred stars from other users
A logo and a screenshot at the top of the repository page
A one-line description and a few topics
A licence badge

prompt: A profile has forty repositories of equal weight. What does the lesson say to do?

choices.text: Delete everything except the portfolio project
Pin the evidence; archive or hide the practice
Add more, so the profile looks busy
Rename them all

prompt: How does a tutorial clone read when it is pinned, by the lesson?

choices.text: As evidence of initiative, since you finished the course on your own time
As your own design
As the course's work
It is not noticed, since reviewers skim past the names

prompt: What does the lesson say a profile README should hold, if you write one?

choices.text: Two lines on what you do and a link to the project
Animated statistics and a wall of badges
choices.why: Cut, for the same reason as in a README.

choices.text: Your CV in full
A list of followers

prompt: What does the contribution graph measure, by the lesson?

choices.text: The number of days you pushed
The quality of your code, judged by the reviews each commit received
Your seniority
How many people follow you

prompt: Your CV says six months on a project, and the graph is empty for those months. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Have the honest answer ready: the work was elsewhere
Fill it with backdated commits
choices.why: Visible, and it reads as what it is.

choices.text: Remove the project from the CV
Hide the graph

prompt: What makes your commits count on the graph, by the lesson?

choices.text: Committing every day at the same hour
An e-mail GitHub links to your account
A paid plan
Signing each commit with a key

prompt: For a support role, which is worth more by the lesson?

choices.text: A year of green squares from exercise commits
Forty public repositories
A profile README with badges
A runbook with a clean history

prompt: A profile pins six course exercises and leaves the portfolio project unpinned, with the description my project. What is the first fix?

choices.text: Add a profile README
Put the real work first, with a one-line summary
Commit daily
Pin more exercises so the six slots show variety across different languages
